title: HT-2: Learn a Walking Trajectory Prior Before Challenging-Terrain Fine-Tuning
content_lines: Source: [arXiv:2410.03654v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.03654v1). Official training code was not public at the audited point, so no source symbols are asserted.

> **Bottom line:** HT-2 first learns a useful locomotion trajectory distribution on easier terrain, then fine-tunes with reinforcement learning on challenging geometry. The staged route improves exploration and gait quality; it does not make terrain perception, unseen obstacles, or hardware safety automatic.
## Engineering problem

Starting terrain RL from random actions yields frequent falls and sparse progress, while training only on flat-ground tracking does not teach foothold adaptation. Learning balance and terrain negotiation simultaneously wastes samples.
## Method

The system pretrains a trajectory-conditioned locomotion capability, then adapts it under terrain observations and task rewards. The prior narrows early exploration to walking-like behavior while RL changes foot placement and body motion for terrain.

## Decisive evidence

Pretrained-versus-scratch learning curves and terrain-specific gait measurements support the staged-training claim. Results should be read per terrain class rather than as one universal robustness score.
## Paper-to-implementation mapping

Without official code, a faithful reimplementation must expose the pretraining dataset/objective, trajectory representation, transfer checkpoint, terrain curriculum, perception input, fine-tuning reward, and reset policy. These interfaces, not invented class names, are the audit targets.
## Limits and evidence boundary

The prior can discourage behaviors absent from pretraining, and simulated terrain sensing can be cleaner than hardware perception. The paper does not guarantee arbitrary obstacles, deformable ground, severe occlusion, or falls outside the tested distribution.
## Bounded engineering takeaway

Separate acquisition of a stable locomotion manifold from terrain specialization, but retain scratch and frozen-prior baselines. Monitor whether the prior improves learning or merely prevents exploration of necessary new contacts.
## Reproduction checklist

Lock pretraining motions, trajectory horizon, checkpoint, terrain generator/split, observations, curriculum, rewards, randomization, and hardware sensing. Report samples-to-threshold, success by terrain, foot placement/slip, torque/impact, perception failures, and interventions.
